clinicalPearls: Defined by autoimmune adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) combined with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus
It is the most common of the autoimmune polyglandular syndromes and typically presents in adulthood, more often in women
Inheritance is polygenic with a strong association with particular HLA haplotypes, unlike the monogenic type 1 syndrome
Component disorders often appear years apart, so a new autoimmune endocrinopathy should prompt vigilance for others
Additional autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and primary gonadal failure are frequently associated
Starting thyroid hormone in an unrecognised adrenal-insufficient patient can precipitate an adrenal crisis, so cortisol status must be assessed first
Periodic screening of at-risk relatives and of affected patients for evolving deficiencies is central to management
Treatment is lifelong hormone replacement tailored to each affected gland
reference.pathophysiology: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which loss of immune self-tolerance leads to lymphocytic destruction of multiple endocrine glands. Susceptibility is polygenic, driven strongly by human leucocyte antigen associations together with other immune-regulatory gene variants, rather than by a single-gene defect. Circulating autoantibodies against adrenal, thyroid and pancreatic islet antigens mark the underlying cell-mediated destruction, which progresses at different rates in different glands, producing the characteristic sequential emergence of adrenal insufficiency, thyroid dysfunction and type 1 diabetes over time.
additionalDifferentials: Type 1 diabetes mellitus without additional endocrinopathy
Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease
IPEX and other monogenic autoimmune syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Morning cortisol with adrenocorticotrophic hormone and short synacthen testing for adrenal insufficiency
Thyroid function tests and thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin and islet-related autoantibodies
Screening for coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia
Assessment of gonadal function where premature failure is suspected
redFlags: Adrenal crisis with hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
Precipitation of crisis by thyroid hormone given before glucocorticoid replacement
Rapid clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and lifelong, appropriately balanced hormone replacement, patients can expect a near-normal life, though the ongoing risk of adrenal crisis and the potential for new autoimmune components to develop necessitate continued surveillance.
pitfalls: Starting levothyroxine before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency and triggering a crisis
Diagnosing a single endocrinopathy without considering the wider syndrome
Failing to screen for evolving deficiencies over time
Overlooking associated non-endocrine autoimmune disease such as coeliac disease
Confusing the polygenic type 2 syndrome with the monogenic type 1 form
management: Lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for autoimmune adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)
Levothyroxine for autoimmune thyroid failure and insulin for associated type 1 diabetes mellitus
Assess and correct adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroid hormone to prevent precipitating adrenal crisis
Patient education in sick-day rules with a steroid emergency card and injectable hydrocortisone for intercurrent illness
Emergency management of adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluid resuscitation
Periodic clinical and autoantibody surveillance for delayed emergence of additional components including coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia and gonadal failure
Endocrinology-led coordination of replacement across multiple failing glands, with counselling of relatives about familial autoimmune risk
